rv.q: Slick as it looks and as well-acted as it is, in sketching out Maneesh and Riley’s efforts to expose Athena, “Data” can also feel sometimes hampered by predictability.
It's a correct if obvious idea, here rendered as didactically as if we're watching a medieval morality play.
Data is impressive in every aspect.
An early contender for the best new play of 2026, Data is essential viewing for anyone who wants to understand the dystopia the AI revolution is leading to, and why it is succeeding.
As such it is one of the most important plays of our time, a cautionary tale that should be seen by all Americans.
Not a gimcrack piece of crime fiction, Data doesn't pretend that the march of new technology can be stopped.
Data is an exciting, frightening look at our increasingly tech-controlled world.
Structurally, Data is not without flaws, but given the urgency of the material, they can easily be overlooked.
This tech thriller explores the ethical dilemmas of big tech and the moral underpinnings of contemporary work culture.

Director Tyne Rafaeli sustains a brisk pace and an air of anxiety that's enhanced between scenes by noise and flash provided by Daniel Kluger's sound design and electronic music and Amith Chandrashaker's lighting.
Libby's dialogue is so staccato sharp that he keeps our interest without having to resort to a romance to muck things up.
The ultimate result is a surface story whose mechanics are not all that plausible, and frankly not as interesting as the fascinating ethical dilemmas that the play explores.
Data is throbbingly enticing, and a truly chilling journey that is important both as a cautionary tale and a depiction of what true heroism looks like in the digital age.
It's gripping enough to command your attention for 100 intermissionless minutes, thanks to Tyne Rafaeli's sharp, sophisticated direction and outstanding performances.
Sure to give you something to discuss on the cab ride home, this is an important piece for right now – so make your way to the Lucile Lortel this winter to catch it.
The stellar Data couldn’t feel more timely and real.

This dark foray into the clash of data code and honor code — where morality is malware and trust isn’t always two-step verified — proves entertaining for viewers already thinking about the information arms race among the world’s largest tech companies.
Brar and Lillis capture the complexity of their characters’ plight, and how easily mutual respect can shift into suspicion and doubt.
Dark, unsettling, and so plausible that it feels ripped from the headlines, Data depicts a world in which the safeguards between us and total government surveillance are flimsy indeed.
It brings up interesting topic of conversation around lofty ideas and real-world implementation.
It is tense, thoughtful, and disturbingly grounded in the present moment.

cn.t: Critics praise "Data" as a timely, intelligent techno-thriller that feels urgently relevant to today's headlines. Matthew Libby's play earns acclaim for its thought-provoking exploration of tech ethics, privacy, and immigration, delivered with suspense and humanity.

vr.q: I would totally recommend this piece — it's educational, thought provoking, and plain old entertaining theatre.
Data is the rare play that I feel like actually manages to speak to the technological concerns of today
